# How much of the web app an agent can do

<!-- Generated by backend/gates/mcpparity_test.go. Do not edit by hand. -->

**85.5%** of what the web app calls for a signed-in user is open to that user's agent through MCP: 731 of 854 operations.
Counting what another tool covers, it is 87.2%. Once every pending operation opens, it is 87.2%. What is left is closed for security, apart from signing out.

## The three counts

| Counted over | Operations | Open to an agent | Parity |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Every operation in the contract | 1027 | 843 | 82.0% |
| Operations a signed-in user reaches | 987 | 843 | 85.4% |
| Operations the web app calls for a signed-in user | 854 | 731 | 85.5% |

The last count answers the question of parity with the web app, so it leads this page. The first adds pages for visitors with no account, where no agent acts because no signed-in user does. The second adds routes where the scan found no web app call: 112 of those are open, so an agent can do them.

| Of the operations the web app calls | Count |
|---|---:|
| Open, and the agent does not ask first | 643 |
| Open, and the agent asks first | 88 |
| Pending | 0 |
| Covered by another tool | 14 |
| Closed for security | 108 |
| Sign-in | 1 |

## What each state means

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Open | The operation carries `x-mcp-tool`, so a user's agent can run it through MCP, with that user's grants. |
| Ask first | Open, and its tool tells the agent to ask its user first (`ask_user_first`). A legal or lasting act stays open this way. |
| Pending | Closed for now. Nothing keeps it closed but the work of opening it. |
| Security | Closed for good: a secret, more rights than the user gave, or a rule the whole company runs on. |
| Covered | Closed as a route, because another tool does the same job. |
| Sign-in | A step of signing in or out, which an agent has no use for. |

The contract says which state applies: `x-mcp-tool`, or `x-agent-access` with `x-human-only-reason` in
`backend/api/crm.yaml`. [an-agent-does-what-its-user-does.md](../principles/an-agent-does-what-its-user-does.md)
says what keeps an action closed. A user's role narrows both doors the same way, so these counts do not change by role.
[mcp-tool-roles.md](mcp-tool-roles.md) shows what each role can do.

## How an operation gets its group

1. An operation no signed-in user's cookie admits is public. This is the rule
   `tools/gen-agentpolicy` holds a human-only operation to.
2. A path rule places it, or the default of its first OpenAPI tag. The table is in
   `backend/gates/mcpparityplaces_test.go`. A tag that spans groups, such as `Identity`, has no default, so a
   new route under it fails the gate until someone places it. So does a new tag.
3. A settings area splits by what the seeded `rep` role may do. A setting it passes goes to the non-admin group,
   and the rest go to the admin group. So one area can have its reads in the first group and its writes in the second.

The answer for `rep` comes from these places, in this order:

- `decided_by: measured`: [mcp-tool-roles.json](mcp-tool-roles.json) ran the real tool on that role. Only a verb that
  serves one operation counts, because a row for a shared verb says nothing about any one route.
- `decided_by: grant_checks`: the checks the handler makes, against [rbac-matrix.md](rbac-matrix.md). The gate walks from
  the method `compose.Server` serves the operation with, and follows `auth.Require`, `auth.RequireAny`,
  `auth.RequireAdmin` and `auth.RequireCoach`. A boolean read such as `auth.Allows` or `auth.ReadGranted`
  refuses nobody by itself, so it counts as conditional.
- `decided_by: no_check`: the walk found no check, so any member passes.
- `decided_by: declared`: `x-settings-audience` in the contract, on an operation where the source cannot answer: its
  object is known only at run time, or a branch decides who a check stops. The gate fails a declaration the source could
  answer, and a missing one where it cannot.

Each operation's group, area, state and how it was decided are in [mcp-parity.json](mcp-parity.json).

## What a scan of the web app can miss

The scan reads `frontend/src` and each unit's `frontend` folder. It leaves out tests and stories. It finds a typed
call such as `api.GET("/path")`, a path held in a constant or a template in the same file and passed to the client, and a
`/v1/` URL used as a link, an image or an upload.

It cannot see these, so the web app's real count may be higher:

- a URL the server sends back, such as a company's `logo_url`;
- a URL built from a variable that holds the `/v1` part;
- a path passed in from another file, listed under `computed_calls_no_path_was_found_for` in the JSON.

It can also count too much: finding a call says the code can make it, and a screen may be hidden behind a feature or
a role. Routes a unit adds under `/ext/` are outside the contract, so they are counted apart.

## Regenerate

The gate fails when these files and their sources disagree, in either direction. From `backend/`:

    go test ./gates -run TestTheMCPParityCatalogIsPublished -update-mcp-parity
